title: Milestone 4 quarto website
text:
This is a Quarto website created for a simple course project.

Visit my local Quarto website



This page uses real public FRED data from the last five years and builds an interactive view of how AI, robotics, and automation pressure may relate to unemployment and labor-market displacement. The chart expands the monthly payroll and unemployment records into thousands of observation rows across sector and occupation risk groups.



The future of work is often described through automation pressure, but the real story is more complex. Jobs that involve repetitive rules, routine data entry, and predictable decisions are often easier for AI and robotics systems to replace or reshape.

Automation tends to affect routine tasks first, not entire occupations instantly.
Some jobs expand when AI handles repetitive tasks and humans focus on judgment, supervision, and customer care.
The strongest workforce transitions happen when workers receive retraining, coaching, and time to learn new digital tools.
The labor market can shift quickly when technology spreads through logistics, customer support, clerical work, and production systems.

The data conversation should be careful: AI and robotics may reduce certain tasks, but they can also create new work in maintenance, oversight, programming, training, and specialized operations.




library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(plotly)

unrate_url <- "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=UNRATE"
payems_url <- "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=PAYEMS"

unrate <- readr::read_csv(unrate_url, show_col_types = FALSE)
payems <- readr::read_csv(payems_url, show_col_types = FALSE)

colnames(unrate) <- c("date", "unemployment_rate")
colnames(payems) <- c("date", "payroll_employment")

labor <- unrate |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2021-09-01")) |>
  left_join(payems |> mutate(date = as.Date(date)), by = "date") |>
  arrange(date)

sectors <- tibble(
  sector = c(
    "Manufacturing", "Food Service", "Retail", "Logistics", "Customer Support",
    "Finance", "Admin", "Education", "Health", "Professional Services",
    "Construction", "Agriculture", "Transport", "Media", "Energy"
  ),
  exposure_index = c(
    82, 74, 68, 77, 71,
    62, 61, 50, 45, 65,
    60, 57, 78, 56, 64
  )
)

occupations <- tibble(
  occupation = c(
    "Routine Production", "Data Entry", "Scheduling", "Warehousing",
    "Retail Support", "Customer Service", "Cashiering", "Transport Coordination",
    "Admin Support", "Quality Checking", "Clerical Review", "Field Inspection"
  ),
  automation_risk = c(
    86, 90, 72, 81,
    79, 71, 76, 78,
    68, 75, 66, 70
  )
)

expanded <- labor |>
  cross_join(sectors) |>
  cross_join(occupations) |>
  mutate(
    months_since_start = as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 30,
    sector_pressure = unemployment_rate * exposure_index / 100,
    occupation_pressure = automation_risk,
    payroll_change = payroll_employment - lag(payroll_employment, default = first(payroll_employment)),
    job_loss_signal = round(
      (sector_pressure * 60) +
      (occupation_pressure * 0.4) +
      (abs(payroll_change) / 100) +
      (unemployment_rate * 10),
      1
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(payroll_employment))

plotly_obj <- plot_ly(
  expanded,
  x = ~date,
  y = ~job_loss_signal,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~sector,
  colors = "Set2",
  marker = list(size = 5, opacity = 0.75, line = list(color = "#ffffff", width = 0.5)),
  hovertemplate = paste(
    "Sector: %{meta}<br>",
    "Occupation: %{customdata}<br>",
    "Month: %{x}<br>",
    "Job-loss signal: %{y}<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~occupation,
  meta = ~sector
) |>
  layout(
    title = "AI, Robotics, and Automation Risk Signal",
    xaxis = list(title = "Month"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Estimated job-loss signal"),
    legend = list(title = list(text = "Sector")),
    paper_bgcolor = "#000000",
    plot_bgcolor = "#000000",
    font = list(color = "#ffffff"),
    template = "plotly_dark"
  )

plotly_obj
